images.title: Halving 60° to get 30° and 15°
images.purpose: Show the finished construction in which a 60° angle is bisected to give 30°, and the 30° is bisected again to give 15°.
images.composition: One finished construction with vertex A at the lower left and the base ray running right along the bottom; the arcs fan out above it, leaving white space on the right and top.
exact_structure: A dark horizontal ray from A to the right, with B on it; A at the lower left, labelled A, and B labelled B.
One large grey (#6B7280) arc centred at A, passing through B, E and C, where C is at 60° above AB and E is at 30° above AB.
A thin dark segment from A to C (the 60° arm), with one small grey (#6B7280) arc of the same radius centred at B meeting the large arc at C.

Two small grey (#6B7280) arcs, one centred at B and one centred at C, crossing at D just beyond the large arc; the ray AD in reddish purple (#CC79A7), passing through E, with a small angle arc between AB and AD labelled 30°.

Two small grey (#6B7280) arcs, one centred at B and one centred at E, crossing at F just beyond the large arc; the ray AF in reddish purple (#CC79A7) drawn a little thinner, with a small angle arc between AB and AF labelled 15°.
Exactly 6 point labels: A, B, C, D, E, F. Exactly 2 angle labels: 30° and 15°.
rejection: the angle marked 30° not exactly half of angle CAB, or the angle marked 15° not exactly half of the 30° angle
arcs drawn in any colour other than grey, or the rays AD and AF not in reddish purple
a protractor, degree scale or any angle label other than 30° and 15°
images.takeaway: Bisecting the 60° angle from an equilateral triangle gives 30°, and bisecting 30° gives 15°.
images.description: A finished compass construction at A: a large grey arc through B, E and C, bisecting arcs meeting at D and F, with reddish purple rays AD at 30° and AF at 15° above AB.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on constructing 30° and 15° angles.
images.teaching_notes: Trace the arcs in order, first to C for 60°, then to D for 30°, then to F for 15°, and point out that each new ray halves the previous angle.

image_decisions.why: The finished construction shows how bisecting 60° and then 30° gives 30° and 15°, which is hard to picture from words alone.
